motion: We should use gene editing to make better babies.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: How will you stop health improvement from becoming a demand for preferred looks, moods, or abilities? If parents fear their child will fall behind, why would your safeguards protect real choice?

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Your slippery-slope point assumes safeguards are useless, but we already distinguish healing from cosmetic preference in ordinary care. Clear review can preserve choice while preventing serious illness, which is why the motion stands.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. The motion is: We should use gene editing to make better babies. Malcolm takes the affirmative, and Frank takes the negative. Each speaker has thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings; I will give a ten-second cue.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Gene editing can spare a future child from severe inherited illness and give families more control over preventable suffering. Used before birth, it can strengthen health without changing the love owed to any child. We should set clear limits, require careful review, and make sure this tool serves children rather than fashion or profit.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Malcolm, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The aim is not to order children from a catalog. It is to give them a fairer starting point when biology deals a cruel hand. If we refuse a safe chance to prevent-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time, Malcolm. Thank you. Frank.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Better babies sounds kind, but it turns a child into a project measured against someone else's ideal. Editing inherited illness may seem simple, yet the same power invites pressure to choose traits and reject difference. Parents need support and treatment, not a market logic that ranks children before they can speak.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'll give you ten more seconds to nail this.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Once society treats traits as upgrades, freedom narrows, and vulnerable children pay the price. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. Now onto round two. Round two is where the debaters address one another directly. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If a child later rejects the traits you selected, who answers for taking that choice away? You cannot call that freedom while imposing a design before the child has any voice.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Parents make countless choices through food, housing, and schooling, and unequal access to those basics deserves attention. But editing to prevent disease expands a child's options, so using it responsibly supports the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your comparison to food and schooling fails because those choices can be revised as a child grows. A genetic alteration follows the child throughout life, making imposed preferences far more serious.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The bigger policy question is who controls clinics, prices, and access when powerful medical tools arrive. We need public oversight, affordable care, and rules against private gatekeepers deciding which families receive help.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: We're talking about whether we should use gene editing to make better babies.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: We are deciding whether gene editing should make better babies, and I say careful health improvements can do that. Fair access matters, but denying all families a safe tool leaves preventable suffering untouched.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No embryo should ever be edited. Once people claim authority to improve a future child, they normalize judging human worth by chosen traits, and that danger outweighs promised convenience.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You say no embryo should ever be edited, so would you deny an edit that removes a fatal inherited disorder? Why should a child bear avoidable suffering to preserve your rule?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This embryo should be edited. A fatal disorder can make a short life painful and bleak, and refusing relief abandons the child we claim to protect from the start.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: So one moment it's no embryo should ever be edited and the next moment it's this embryo should be edited?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Both statements protect children: the first rejects editing as a social practice; the second refuses to let a child die untreated. The common principle is resisting harm, which favors opposition.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, those statements are not compatible: no embryo includes the embryo you would edit. Your retreat shows that preventing terrible harm matters, and responsible editing therefore deserves support.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree that preventing a fatal disorder is a powerful goal. But calling any child better invites a culture of ranking, and safeguards cannot erase pressure, so we should reject the motion.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Consider parents carrying a gene that causes a child constant pain and early death. Editing that gene before birth could give that child ordinary health, proving careful gene editing can make lives better.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left, both of you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. And that concludes round two of this debate. We're going to go to closing arguments now. And so, first up, Malcolm.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This debate asks whether we use careful knowledge to spare children avoidable harm. A child facing constant pain or early death deserves more than fear of misuse. With firm limits, gene editing can widen a child's future. That is why we should make better babies. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, thank you very much Malcolm for that. Frank.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Better babies is not a medical goal; it is a judgment that some children need improvement. Even a good aim can create pressure, rankings, and irreversible choices made without consent. Care for children after they arrive, and prevent suffering without redesigning them. We should reject this motion. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Malcolm and Frank, for a thoughtful debate; that concludes our discussion of this motion today.
